en: The *Sutra of the Pure Avalokiteśvara-Bhadracari Dhāraṇī*, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhitong of Zongchi Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Vulture Peak in the city of Rājagṛha.
The Buddha was together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus and an incalculable number of bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was seated together with ninety-two koṭis of bodhisattvas.
Then, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara...
In the early morning, he rose from his seat,
adjusted his robes, joined his palms in reverence,
prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I wish to recite the Samantabhadra Dhāraṇī.
Out of compassion and for the benefit of all sentient beings,
I received this spell from the Buddha Candraprabha in the past.”
Now I wish to recite this dhāraṇī before the Buddha.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave to speak it.
Then he spoke the mantra, saying:
Namo Aḍḍatālarājāya. Namo Ārya-Vairocani-Spharaṇāya. Bodhisattvāya. Mahāsattvāya. Mahākāruṇikāya. Tadyathā.

9. *Siddhānta-baddha-dhāraṇī* (50). *Svāhā* (51). The above is the root mantra.
The *dhāraṇī* for binding the boundary is as follows:

*Namo hradatantrāya | namo ārya-vairocani-spharaṇāya | bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya | tadyathā | jili-panṭe mi | mili-panṭe mi | jili-mili-panṭe mi | sima-panṭe mi | sima-mameka-ścid-dhati-makarama-du | svāhā.* Recite this mantra twenty-one times over water and sprinkle it in the ten directions; the boundary is thereby established.
Regarding this dhāraṇī mantra,
one must first receive and maintain it to establish a boundary in advance;
if one establishes the boundary as I have done, success will be attained.
The invocation of the dhāraṇī is as follows:

*Namo ratnatrayāya.* *Namo ārya-avalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya.* *Tadyathā:* *ciri ciri* *miri miri* *cirili* *hūṃ bhagavan āryāvalokiteśvarāya svāhā.* If one wishes to invoke me, [one should recite this].
As I have taught, after having made the mental supplication,
from the eighth day to the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight,
one should bathe daily three times with fragrant water and wear fresh, clean garments.
Recite this mantra one hundred and eight times each at the three periods of every day.
On the fifteenth day, perform a particularly superior offering and recite it without limit.
Then, at midnight that very night, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will appear.
He will spontaneously appear in a body of golden hue, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence,
emitting various lights and a thousand rays of radiance.
At that time, the mantra-practitioner must not feel fear in his heart.
Once the practitioner has seen this and attained the dharani-samadhi of the Supreme Ground,
they immediately behold the Buddha Akṣobhya in the east and the Buddha Ratnaketu in the south.
In the west is Amitābha Buddha, and in the north is Subhavyūha Buddha;
they behold such infinite Buddhas, Tathāgatas, throughout the ten directions, with their radiant colors and physical marks.
Having cast off this body, one will be born in a pure buddha-field praised by all Buddhas in every place.
Thus concludes the exposition of the Samantabhadra Dhāraṇī.
At that time, when the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara had finished speaking this mantra,
ninety-two koṭis of bodhisattvas all attained the stage of avaivartika.
Furthermore, they shall behold all Buddhas and hear the True Dharma;
they shall extinguish all heavy offenses of the three obstructions and attain great merit,
equal in number to the atoms of dust upon the ground of Jambudvīpa.
The practitioner themselves will attain various adornments of merit;
all illnesses, sufferings, and evil karmas will be completely extinguished.
Furthermore, they will attain swift eloquence and a sovereign mind that fulfills all vows according to their wishes.
They shall attain the fulfillment of all the pāramitās;
according to their wishes, they shall be reborn in the pure lands of the ten directions,
where they shall behold all Buddhas and hear them preach the True Dharma.
They attained all samādhis such as Śūraṅgama,
as well as the Seven-Jewels Samādhi, the Radiating-Light Samādhi,
the Great-Ocean-Water Samādhi, the Sky-Ascending Samādhi, and the Appearing-and-Vanishing Samādhi.
One attains such samādhis as these, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River,
and further attains immeasurable gateways of great-power dhāraṇīs.
The merit of this mantra is no different from the merit of eight hundred thousand dhāraṇīs.
By the power of this mantra, may I attain such a Dharma-body and be able to benefit all sentient beings;
may I swiftly attain various forms of intelligence, eloquence, and the pure Dharma-body.
By the power of this mantra, upon hearing it once, one will never again forget the dhāraṇī.
By the power of this mantra, wherever the snares I have cast may bind,
the heavy sins of all sentient beings shall be extinguished.
All evil persons, as well as evil māras, evil ghosts, and evil deities,
will naturally submit and be extinguished.
All sentient beings who hear the name of this dhāraṇī and those who receive and uphold it [shall likewise attain these benefits].
They shall never fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! By the power of this mantra of yours, if there are members of the fourfold assembly who are able to receive and uphold it..."
The merit they shall attain and their majestic power will be no different from my own.
At that time, when the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara spoke this mantra,
the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
Upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven,
all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and all spirits, ghosts, humans, and non-humans therein.
All were terrified and their body hairs stood on end;
they praised him, saying, "Excellent! The spiritual power of this mantra is inconceivable.
All sentient beings shall receive its benefit."
Then Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May the Buddha bear witness that it is well;
may the fourfold assembly [bear witness] to the dhāraṇī spoken by me."
Everyone should apply their minds to receive, uphold, revere, and make offerings to it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I shall now receive and uphold this mantra."
The entire great earth shook in six ways;
all sentient beings, as well as the devas and nāgas, were utterly alarmed and terrified.
The spiritual power of this mantra is inconceivable.
By what causes and conditions shall I and all sentient beings who uphold [this] attain the Vajra Samādhi,
and cause you and all sentient beings [to do likewise]?
Those who uphold it will attain peace and stability of mind;
the merit they obtain and their spiritual power will be no different from my own.
I shall further explain the efficacy of this mantra.
Recite the mantra twenty-one times at dawn,
twenty-one times at midday,
and twenty-one times toward evening.
By constantly upholding this without forgetting, one can eliminate the grave sins of the five heinous acts.
Furthermore, one will achieve all samādhis, such as the Śūraṅgama, and also achieve all dhāraṇīs.
Furthermore, one will achieve all Buddha-dharmas.
If one can constantly apply the mind to recitation and mindfulness without forgetting,
one will always see Śākyamuni Buddha and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
One should contemplate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and see the goddesses requesting to receive the Buddha-dharma;
if one wishes to create an image [of them], [one should do so accordingly].
One should depict Śākyamuni Buddha seated upon a lotus throne,
his body golden-yellow in color and wearing robes of five colors.
On the left side, paint the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra seated upon Mount Sumeru.
On the left side of that mountain, there were seven-headed nāgas encircling it;
from the left side, seven heads emerged,
gazing toward the Bodhisattva.
On the right side, five-headed dragons encircle the mountain;
from the right side, five heads emerge,
gazing toward the Bodhisattva.
That bodhisattva sits in the full lotus posture,
holding a scripture between his two hands to read while wearing robes of five colors.
That Buddha forms a mudrā with his right hand.
With his left hand holding the *kāṣāya* robe pressed against his knee, he preaches the Dharma.
On the right side is painted Avalokiteśvara seated upon a lotus throne,
wearing white garments and kneeling with palms joined in *añjali*.
Facing the Buddha, he gazes at and listens to the Buddha preaching the Dharma.
On his left side are three hands;
one hand holds a flower.
With one hand he holds a ritual pitcher (*śīrṣaka*),
with another hand he holds a scripture-case (*tāla-patra*);
on his right side are three hands.
With one hand he bestows fearlessness and produces jewels;
with another hand he holds a lasso, and with another hand he holds a jewel.
Above the head of the Bodhisattva, there is also a Buddha facing him.
The practitioner below kneels on the ground,
burns incense, and holds a rosary while gazing toward the Bodhisattva.
Below Samantabhadra is the goddess Vidyādevī;
she sits in the hukuili posture, holding a flower crown in her hands,
and wears white robes while seated upon a mat.
Look toward the Bodhisattva.
The image must be painted with pure materials and no glue;
the painting must follow the pure dharma.
Next, the method for entering the *dāna* and receiving the precepts is explained.
On the eighth day of the waxing moon, one enters the *maṇḍala*.
Using cow dung, one smears the ground to construct the altar.
The initial [mandala] shall be made in five colors, measuring four cubits up to eight cubits.
One must prepare sixteen jars filled with water, flowers, and fruit;
likewise, sixteen incense burners and sixteen oil lamps are required.
If one constructs a mandala measuring four cubits, place four jars,
four incense burners, and four oil lamps.
One should offer various kinds of food, fruits, clarified butter, honey, and rock sugar;
burn diverse incenses without ceasing throughout the six periods of the day and night.
The practitioner shall bathe and put on clean robes in accordance with the Dharma.
One may eat only polished rice, gruel, milk, curd, butter, honey, fruits, rock sugar, dried ginger, black pepper, and *pi-pa* (dates);
other foods and drinks are not permitted.
From the offerings made to the Buddha on the eighth day until the fifteenth day, the items shall not be collected.
On the sixteenth day, they are gathered and either cast into water or burned by fire.
Then, one returns to the beginning and enters the ritual arena again on the eighth day.
In front of the Buddha altar,
construct another altar measuring one cubit, using cow dung as the base material.
Take dry grain-wood and mulberry wood.
Take one piece [of the material], recite the mantra once over it, and place it within the altar.
Continue this until twenty-one repetitions are completed.
Thereafter, take seven kinds of grain seeds.
Take the mantra with one's hand and recite it once, casting it into the fire;
continue this up to twenty-one times.
This may be done during the day or at night in the darkness.
From one day until the fifteenth, burn the *mōbō* (forget-not) incense once daily; on the night of the fifteenth, do not sleep, but recite the mantra with single-minded concentration.
During that night, the earth may sometimes shake, or a great sound may be heard.
The practitioner should not give rise to alarm or wonder.
Calming the mind, they should recite the mantra while mindful of the two Bodhisattvas.
At that time, Samantabhadra and Avalokiteśvara—
He then spoke to those who practice through body and speech:
"Whatever vow you require, I shall fulfill it for you upon request;
yet, if you do not behold me as you desire, [your purpose will not be met]."
On the sixteenth day, dismantle the altar and construct a new one;
perform the ritual practices and recite the mantras according to the previous method.
This continues until one attains the vision of Pūrṇamanoratha as the limit.
When the practitioner enters the maṇḍala,
they may see only a single person with whom they are permitted to converse.
Others must neither speak nor look [at the practitioner].
The practitioner within the *maṇḍala* must also not speak;
if it is necessary to speak, one must wait until exiting the *maṇḍala*.
The Sutra on the Pure Avalokiteśvara-Bhadracari Dhāraṇī,
Complete with the Ritual for the Avalokiteśvara-Bhadracari Dhāraṇī.
